label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
# I'm not dropping the busing project

Short version, so nobody has to scroll: a parent complained about the busing oral history project, Dr. Halvorsen asked me to drop it, and I told him I wasn't going to. We meet Thursday at 3:15, with the parent in the room. I meant to say this once, properly, instead of having it in fifteen texts, so I'm writing it down instead.

Some of you already know most of this. Jess, this is mostly for you.

## The assignment

Juniors, US History II, two sections. The project: interview someone in your family or your neighborhood about Boston busing and desegregation, 1974 through '76. A ten-minute recording and a two-page reflection. That's it.

This is my fourth year running it at Cobb Street. Four years, a couple hundred kids, and this is the first complaint I've had — the first complaint about anything I've assigned, actually, and I include the ones about essay length.

The complaint came by email to Halvorsen, with a school committee member copied. Two phrases have stayed with me: that the project "reopens wounds," and that it "pressures kids to judge their grandparents."

I'm not going to sit here and pretend I think she's wrong about the second part. She's not. I do put kids in a position where they can be handed a question they weren't ready for — where the assignment turns into something about their own family, their own house, their own dinner table. I have watched a kid go quiet in a way that has nothing to do with the cold. She's noticed something real, and I don't think she noticed it as a gotcha. She noticed it because she pays attention to her kid.

## Two kids, and why I still think this is worth doing

In 2023, a student I'll call D. interviewed his grandmother for this project. She drove a school bus out of Southie in 1974. She had never told anyone in the family that she did it — the interview was the first time it came out of her mouth, and I think it came out of her mouth because the question was asked by somebody who wasn't her family and wasn't judging her.

He played forty seconds of it for the class. Nobody said a word for about a minute. Then I moved on, because that's what you do, you keep the room moving. But I remember the minute.

Last spring, a girl in my other section found out something about her own uncle — that he'd thrown rocks at one of the buses in '74. She was upset. We talked after class twice. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year, and I'll tell you why: she wrote it honestly. Not bravely, not performatively. She wrote what she actually felt, which included being angry at her uncle and loving him at the same time, which is the actual truth and also the hardest thing on earth to put on a page. That's the assignment. That's the whole assignment.

If you take one thing from this post, take that: the students who have the hardest time with this are usually the ones who need it most, and they are also usually the ones who produce the most valuable work. But I don't get to force anybody. That's the line, and it's the line I've always tried to hold.

## What I'm doing instead of backing down

I'm keeping the project. I'm also adding an alternate option, so that no kid *has* to interview family. Any student can:

- interview a librarian, an archivist, or a neighborhood historian instead — the BPL's local history collection, the South Boston Historical Society, the newspapers, the court record, people who were there and weren't your relatives;
- work from recorded interviews from previous years of this project, with permission from the families — including D.'s grandmother, who has now heard her own voice on a school recording;
- or do a document-based version, primary sources and a written reflection, no recording, no interview.

Same learning. Same reflection length. Nobody gets put on the spot, and nobody has to make their grandmother talk about her life to satisfy a teacher.

Here's the thing I want to be clear about: I'm not arguing with the parent. I'm not trying to win a fight with her, and Thursday isn't a tribunal. Halvorsen isn't out to get me — he asked me to drop it quietly, which is a reasonable thing to ask a building leader who has a parent emailing a school committee member. I get it. But "quietly" is exactly the part I can't do, because quiet is how thirty kids never find out that the history in their textbook — the one paragraph, between the Jacksonian period and the oil crisis — was actually made of people.

## Jess

You texted me last night that it's one assignment, don't torch your job over it, and about half the group chat agreed with you.

You're not wrong. I could get burned. I'm tenured, but let's not romanticize that — Halvorsen still sets my schedule and still decides who gets AP next year, and he doesn't need to want to hurt me for that to matter. That's just how a building works, and you know it better than I do, because you were inside one for years.

You and I met as student teachers in 2012, at a school with a heating system that should have been illegal. You left teaching in 2019 and you do HR at a biotech in Cambridge now, which is a whole different kind of meeting with a whole different kind of cost. I hear you. Honestly, I think the reason the group chat is half in agreement is that you're credible in a way I'm not, and because you're being kind about it, which somehow makes it harder to argue with.

But here's why. These kids live in the city. That's the part nobody outside this building gets. Roxbury and Southie and Charlestown and Brighton — the buses ran through all of it, and the arguments are still in the parking lots at the parents' nights. My kids are going to be the ones voting on the housing and the schools and the buses for the next thirty years, and they are learning about it from a paragraph in a textbook that makes it sound like a traffic dispute. The oral history project is the only time in a kid's school career that they sit across from somebody who was actually there and ask them what it was like. There is no other version of this, and there is no way to get it from a book.

## The part I'd rather not write

I'm scared. Not in the noble sense — in the "lying awake thinking about my schedule next year" sense. I'm not going to pretend Thursday is nothing.

But I'm also not going to be the teacher who quietly drops the thing because it made one person uncomfortable and one person uncomfortable can, with one email, make me careful for the rest of the year. That is a very expensive trade, and I don't think it's the right one, and I'm not brave enough to be sure it's the right one, but I'm sure enough to walk into the room Thursday at 3:15 with the alternate assignment printed out and the reflections in my folder and a clear head.

I'm going to walk in there and say to her: you're right, kids shouldn't be pressured, and I've built a version of this that doesn't pressure anybody. And I want her there as a person, not as an obstacle. She probably knows something about her own family's busing story that I've never asked about, and Thursday might be the first time anybody has asked her.

## Thursday

I'll text you after the meeting, Jess. Whatever happens — good, bad, somewhere in the middle, which is the likeliest outcome and the one I have no real plan for.

And if you ever want to come back into a classroom and sit in on a session, the door's open. We've got a shelf of recorded interviews going back years that nobody knows what to do with, and I'd like that to be a problem we share. You know where I am.

Thanks for reading this, and for the texts — even the ones that made me roll my eyes a little. See you Thursday.
